articles.title: Matthew White on WNO's Madama Butterfly
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with tenor Matthew White about the Washington National Opera's production of Puccini's Madama Butterfly.
articles.body:
The interview can also be heard on WETA Virtuoso on the following times:

11/11/2026 8:59PM
11/13/2026 4:57PM

And on WETA VivaLaVoce on the following times:

11/12/2026 10:02AM
11/15/2026 9:57AM

Matthew White, who’s currently singing the role of B. F. Pinkerton in Washington National Opera’s production of Puccini’s Madama Butterfly, didn’t start studying voice until he was nineteen. Before that he played several different instruments in a variety of styles and genres, though classical violin was what he assumed would be his main focus as his teens progressed and he thought about college and career. But when he decided to switch his attention to his voice, he dropped out of college and performed manual labor to support his voice lessons, focusing exclusively on technique for three years before considering repertoire. This bold move paid off; he went on to win a slew of competitions and enjoy a still-ascendant career. (You can find out more in my illuminating interview with him embedded above.) His performance as Pinkerton marks his WNO debut.

articles.title: DC Composer James Lee III
articles.dek: Linda Carducci speaks with Maryland-based composer James Lee III about his visions and influences, his compositions, and his thoughts for the evolving nature of Classical music.
articles.body:
If you attend concerts in the Washington area, chances are you’ve heard the sensitive and inventive music of composer James Lee III. The Maryland-based composer’s works, ranging from orchestral and chamber music to pieces for piano, voice and chorus, have been showcased internationally and described by The Washington Post as "bright, pure music" Major American orchestras, including the National Symphony Orchestra and the Detroit Symphony Orchestra have championed Mr. Lee’s works, and he served as composer-in-residence with the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra for the 2024-2025 season.

As part of our local composers’ spotlight this month of November, we’re pleased to showcase compositions of James Lee III on WETA Classical and WETA’s HD channel, Virtuoso. He discusses his visions and influences, his compositions, and his thoughts for the evolving nature of Classical music, in my conversation with him below.

articles.title: Opera Lafayette Celebrates Rameau 350
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with Artistic Director of Opera Lafayette, Patrick Dupre Quigley, about their Rameau 350 project, starting with Les Surprises des l'Amour this month.
articles.body:
The interview can be heard on WETA Virtuoso on the following times:

11/9/2026 2:59PM
11/10/2026 9:18AM
11/12/2026 4:57AM

The interview can also be heard on WETA VivaLaVoce on the following time:

11/13/2026 4PM

Last month the hot ticket in DC was Oliver Cotton’s play The Score, which took place in 1747. Ostensibly the origin story for Johann Sebastian Bach’s Musical Offering, its climactic scene depicted Bach confronting Frederick the Great about the brutal effects his military campaign had on ordinary citizens.

In the following year, 1748, the War of Austrian Succession finally ended with Aix-la-Chapelle, which also has connections to notable musical compositions. In England, Handel composed the Music for the Royal Fireworks to commemorate the event (and while its premiere resulted in war-like consequences that seemed at odds with its celebration of piece – a building burned down, at least five people suffered serious injuries, and it caused one of the first recorded traffic jams – everyone still liked the music.)

In France, meanwhile, King Louis XV’s illustrious mistress Madame de Pompadour was running her third season of opera and drama in a makeshift theater in her apartment at Versailles. The venue’s very limited seating made admission extremely coveted among the Parisian aristocracy, and while their desire to attend may have been driven by social status, they were from all reports performances of very high quality, including onstage appearances by the Madame herself.

The Aix-la-Chapelle treaty inspired her to commission the most successful living French composer at the time, Jean-Philippe Rameau, for an opera. While his works for the Paris Opéra could run three hours or more, for this occasion he provided a 90-minute work in a prologue and two acts, Les surprises de l'Amour. The one character who ties the work together is Cupid; in the prologue it is revealed that Vulcan’s arrows of war are transformed into Cupid’s arrows of love. The theme of the opera is that love is the rebuke to the cold-heartedness that leads to war – a powerful statement for a mistress to present to the King.

After its initial performance in Madame de Pompadour’s apartment, Les surprises de l'Amour was heavily revised and expanded for performance at the Paris Opéra, and all of its references to the peace treaty were cut. While this later version has been revived and recorded in modern times, the more intimate and philosophical original version has lain on the shelf – until now. Opera Lafayette is giving what it is billing as the “modern world premiere” of the original version of 1748.

I got to speak with Patrick Dupre Quigley, Opera Lafayette’s new artistic director, about this production and their Rameau350 project in a fascinating interview you can hear above.

articles.title: Forward Thinking Opera Company IN Series' New Home in Southwest DC
articles.dek: Evan Keely speaks with IN Series Artistic Director Timothy Nelson about the exciting new chapter of a permanent home at Revada Performing Arts Center in SW DC.
articles.body:
In the history of arts in our nation’s capital, I expect that October 23, 2026 will be a date remembered with appreciation: the date of the Ribbon Cutting for the Revada Arts Center.

This new arts hub in the SW neighborhood, around the corner from the Waterfront Metro stop, will be the home of Theater Alliance, the 4EYE Film Center, and the opera company IN Series. It is the product of the visionary aspirations of the creatives in these three organizations and the surrounding community, and of the generous responses to a $4.5 million capital campaign.

I spoke with Timothy Nelson, Artistic Director of IN Series, about this exciting new development.

articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with DC-based composer Greg Sandow about his works and highlights his album "Three Quartets" recorded by Terra String Quartet.
articles.body:
You can hear this interview followed by works from his album Three Quartets on WETA Virtuoso on these following times:

Greg Sandow has degrees from Harvard and Yale and has taught at Juilliard, Eastman and Peabody. He began his musical life as a singer and focused on composition in college, but he spent most of his career as a writer. He was the classical music critic for the Village Voice and a regular contributor to the Wall Street Journal, and he's also written about pop music and scientific phenomena. This vibrant 83-year-old Washington, D.C. resident has turned his focus back to composition, and I recently spoke to him about a new album of his string quartets performed by the Terra String Quartet. While the three works were conceived separately, Mr. Sandow was pleased to discover how well they work as an album.

articles.title: The Revada Arts Center: A brand-new home for the arts in Southwest DC
articles.dek: Nicole Lacroix speaks with Theater Alliance's executive artistic director Shanara Gabrielle about the opening of a new performing arts space in Southwest DC.
articles.body:
In February of 2025, I happened to be walking home from the library, when I noticed a sign for a play being presented that afternoon by Theater Alliance. The play, "Garbologists," was held in a pop-up black box in the bowels of a brand-new apartment building. This summer, in Waterfront Park, Theater Alliance presented a Woody Guthrie musical. Now, with the grand opening of the Revada Arts Center, Theater Alliance is no longer relagated to pop-ups or the great outdoors.

I met with Theater Alliance's executive artistic director Shanara Gabrielle, a magnetic and passionate advocate, to tour the new complex. We discussed her dreams for this collaborative concept which also includes two other partners, the innovative opera company, INSeries and 4 Eye Film Center (named after the address, 4th and I streets).

We began the tour in the lobby, or as Shanara put it:

"This is the "radical hospitality hub," this will be our co-working and artist networking space as well as our café and community space. We'll have community meetings, really nice coffee and a bar also in the evening. This is also where we hope, when people come to a show, that they want to stay and have a conversation afterwards....that's one of our greatest hopes, that you leave with more questions than you came with."

Nicole Lacroix: During the week, Thursday-Sunday noon to 10 pm, the hub is open to both community and artists...it's a third space where you can bring your computer, get a cup of coffee or tea and absorb the artistic vibes.

There's a grille above the bar on the mezzanine level, where you can watch the labor that goes into producing the plays and operas.

Next, Shanara took me through a portal into the main performance space, the fully-equipped Black Box which seats 140.

articles.title: Ariel Quartet Plays Late Beethoven
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with Ariel Quartet's violist Jan Grüning about completing their Beethoven cycle with their release of the third and final recording of Beethoven's string quartets.
articles.body:
This interview can also be heard on WETA Virtuoso on the following times:

10/26/2026 9:01AM
10/28/2026 5:59AM
10/29/2026 20:59PM
11/1/2026 6:58AM

This month – October 2026 – marks the 200th anniversary of the composition of Beethoven’s final complete work, the String Quartet in F major, Op. 135, and next March is the 200th anniversary of his death. These milestones are part of the reason for the timing of the release of the third and final volume of Beethoven’s quartets by the Ariel Quartet. The cycle has gotten rave reviews in many publications including Gramophone and The New York Times.

The Ariel Quartet was founded in 1998, when its members were teenagers. In 2012 they began their ongoing relationship with the University of Cincinnati College Conservatory of Music, where they serve as faculty quartet-in-residence. That was also the year the quartet had its only personnel change to date when violist Jan Grüning joined the group. He’s definitely committed to it, since he’s married to its cellist Amit Even-Tov and they have three daughters, whom the two violinists, Gershon Gerchikov and Alexandra Kazovsky, know very well. It’s a very tight-knit ensemble – which one has to be to tackle Beethoven’s late quartets.

They are almost frighteningly intimate. It’s telling that after his twin peaks - the Missa Solemnis and the Ninth Symphony - works that required some of the largest musical forces that had ever been assembled up to that time – Beethoven spent the three years remaining to him composing one last cycle of string quartets. It’s a true cycle, with shared themes and references across all five works: the Quartet in E flat, op. 127; the Quartet in a minor, op. 132, which contains the sublime Heiliger Dankgesang (“Holy Song of Thanksgiving”), a musical prayer of gratitude for surviving a severe illness; the Quartet in B flat, op. 130, a massive work in six movements that the Ariel plays with its original finale, the Grosse Fuge, which gave its first listeners a kind of sneak preview of the quartets of Bartok and Shostakovich they would not live long enough to hear; the Quartet in c sharp minor, op, 131 a cyclic work in seven uninterrupted movements that Beethoven declared was his greatest composition; and the Quartet in F major, op. 135, an unexpected return to Haydnesque dimensions, but underneath its classical surface is a work just as deep and mysterious as the others – the finale is based on an inscrutable motif that Beethoven indicates is supposed to evoke the phrase “Muss es sein?” (“Must it be?”), ending his body of work with what is either a profound existential question or a silly joke, or both. (The Ariel decided not to include in this set the alternative finale to op. 130, but they have indicated that it will be included on an upcoming album.)

The Ariel Quartet has been playing the late quartets since the beginning of their career, and one can tell; they fully inhabit this music which they know as well as they know one another.

articles.title: Actor Jamie Wilkes on Playing C.P.E. Bach on STC's The Score
articles.dek: James Jacobs speaks with actor Jamie Wilkes about playing C.P.E. Bach in STC's production of The Score, a play surrounding the musical challenge proposed to J.S. Bach resulting in the Musical Offering.
articles.body:
Jamie Wilkes is currently playing Carl Philip Emanuel Bach in Oliver Cotton’s The Score, currently playing at STC Shakespeare Theatre Company starring Brian Cox as his character’s father Johann Sebastian Bach. He received his professional training at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Arts – the same school where, half a century earlier, Mr. Cox received his training. This actually helped Wilkes get into character, because he was a long-time admirer of the elder actor’s work and looked up to him as a legend he hoped to emulate, much like CPE Bach’s relationship to JS Bach. That was just one of many fascinating observations he revealed to me in our interview (which you can listen to in the embedded audio). Jamie’s trajectory does in fact bear much resemblance to Brian’s: they have both worked at many of the same theatres and institutions, from the Edinburgh Fringe to the Royal Shakespeare Company, and Jamie has already accrued an impressive body of work in what Americans call “prestige television” and the Brits just call television, including a recurring role on His Dark Materials for HBO/BBC One.

articles.title: Pulitzer Prize-Winning Ellen Taaffe Zwilich on Her Music
articles.dek: John Banther speaks with the first woman composer to win the Pulitzer Prize in Music, Ellen Taaffe Zwilich, about her music, including The Peanuts Gallery composed in honor of her feature on the comic strip.
articles.body:
On a recent episode of Classical Breakdown, your guide to classical music, we talked about Peanuts Gallery, a piano concerto by Ellen Taaffe Zwilich, a Pulitzer Prize winning American composer. It brings all the Peanuts characters to life, and in that episode, we learned all about the music and how different art forms come together in culture.

I also recently spoke with this composer, we talked about several of her works, and when you listen to the interview on WETA Virtuoso (see On Air This Week for the schedule), we’ll also hear one of the works afterwards.

A new work by Damien Geter gets its Washington premiere on October 24 at the Anna H. Wang Concert Series. It’s called Declaration, features J’Nai Bridges with a libretto by Aaron Dworkin, and marks both the 30th anniversary of the Sphynx Organization and the 250th of the United States of America.

Damien and I will give a pre-concert talk this Saturday beforehand to discuss the details, but to get us ready for that and the world premiere, he went ahead and gave us an idea as to what we can expect in this work and each movement.

articles.title: Davóne Tines' Recital No. 1: Mass on Fortas Chamber Music Concerts
articles.dek: Bass-baritone Davóne Tines opens Fortas Chamber Music Concerts with Recital No. 1: MASS, both a recital and theatrical work exploring spirituality, history, identity and renewal.
articles.body:
Bass-baritone Davóne Tines self-describes — quite accurately — as “a singer and creator”, for this artist is more than just an exceptionally gifted vocalist. These qualities will be evident in his performance on Wednesday, October 14 at the Fortas Chamber Music Concerts of his Recital No. 1: MASS. This is a recital, yes, but also a theatrical work, and a personal and communal exploration of spirituality, history, identity and renewal. Tines has performed it at the Ojai Music Festival in 2022. In this Washington performance, he will be joined by pianist John Bitoy III.

Recital No. 1: MASS is not, strictly speaking, a performance of a musical setting of the Roman Catholic Mass Ordinary, though it does contain elements of that tradition — while invoking many other voices, customs, spiritualities and experiences as well. Johann Sebastian Bach makes an appearance, with one of the most beloved arias from the Saint Matthew Passion; Margaret Bonds and Julius Eastman, Black American composers of the 20th century, are represented; compositions by Tyshawn Sorey and Caroline Shaw will be featured.

The concert will be in the Hammer Auditorium, inside the Flagg Building at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design.

articles.title: On Brahms and Bonds with The Thirteen's Matthew Robertson
articles.dek: Evan Keely and The Thirteen's Artistic Director Matthew Robertson share an insight into Brahms' German Requiem and Bond's Credo ahead of The Thirteen's first concert of the season, Brahms and Bonds.
articles.body:
Recently I sat down with Matthew Roberston, founder and Artistic Director of The Thirteen, to talk with him about their October performances of Johannes Brahms’s Ein Deutsches Requiem, and Credo by American composer Margaret Bonds.

Few choral works have achieved the near-universal acclaim of the “German Requiem” Brahms completed in 1868. The Thirteen will present it in the composer’s own edition with piano four-hands; Eric Conway and Brian Ganz (who completed his monumental Chopin project earlier this year) will be the pianists.

Bonds’s Credo is not as well-known as it deserves to be, though that appears — felicitously — to be changing. It is a choral setting of a 1904 text by W. E. B. Du Bois. It’s première was here in Washington in 1967; another early performance was conducted by Zubin Mehta in Los Angeles in 1972, shortly after the composer’s death. I had occasion to become better acquainted with this work when I produced a program on Bonds for WETA Virtuoso for Black History Month this past February. I am not aware of another commercially available recording of this magnificent work other than the 2023 album by the Dessoff Choirs, which has been featured on WETA Classical’s Choral Showcase and on WETA VivaLaVoce.

programs.name: WETA Virtuoso Lunchtime Concert
programs.desc: Live recorded performances from the finest orchestras in the U.S. and around the world, Monday through Thursday from 12-2 PM. These Lunchtime Concerts showcase the artistry and energy of live performance and connect WETA Virtuoso listeners to concert halls across the globe. Fridays take a more intimate turn with chamber music followed by an exploration of early music, offering a perfect midday escape into classical music's diverse landscape.
